transcript.text:
Enrollment forms come in from the HCP office by fax or through the provider portal. Our hub
vendor, Meridian, picks them up and keys the PEF into Atlas. Meridian also checks whether the
patient is already in the system, and if they are, they figure out what to do with it.

They check the diagnosis code on the form against the approved codes. If it's off-label they
send it back to the office.

If anything is missing from the form, the PAM follows up with the office until it's complete.
The HIPAA section has to be signed before we can do anything with the patient.

Once the form is complete, a case is created and assigned by territory, and the patient moves
on to BV.

Thanks — that gives me a clear spine for the main flow: a form arrives, Meridian keys it into Atlas, you check for an existing patient, check the diagnosis code, chase anything missing, then create and assign a case before the patient moves on to BV. A few quick questions about the program as a whole will tell me which branches to dig into, and I'd also like to pin down what actually happens once you spot a duplicate.

questions.text: Do any of the products in this program have a REMS?
Does the program offer nurse or clinical educator support?
Can a patient start an enrollment themselves, without the HCP?

transcript.text: Nope, none of the products in this program have REMS. The program does not offer nurse or clinical educator support. No a patient cannot do that.

Thanks — that's helpful, and I've kept your note that the HIPAA section has to be signed before anything can be done with the patient. I'd like to firm up one screening question, then come back to what Meridian actually does when they spot an existing patient, since the flow leaves that open.

questions.text: Does the program enroll any patients under 18?

When Meridian finds the patient is already in the system, what do they actually do with it — for example attach it to the existing patient, treat it as a new product, or something else? Does each of those go down a different path?
You mentioned the HIPAA section is signed on the form — are there other consents collected from the patient, and are there other ways consent can be captured if that form section isn't signed?

transcript.text: No it does not. They attach it to the existing patient. We capture text and email consent. If that form isn't signed, we will follow up and send a DocuSign link to them.

Thanks — that settles the screening questions, so I won't need to branch for REMS, nurse support, self-enrollment or minors. Let me fill in the front of the main flow next: where new forms wait, what record gets created, and how the prescriber gets linked.

questions.text: Once a form comes in by fax or the provider portal, where does it sit before Meridian starts working it — is there a queue or inbox it lands in, and is it one pool for both channels?
When Meridian keys the PEF into Atlas, what kind of record gets created for the person at that point, and does that record change type or status later?
How is the prescriber found and linked to the patient's record, and which identifiers are used to match them?

transcript.text: Thanks — I've captured that a matched submission is attached to the existing patient, that you collect text and email consent, and that an unsigned HIPAA section means a follow-up with a DocuSign link. I'll keep moving through the main line now and pin down the prescription rule and the ways a submission can end without the patient being enrolled.

questions.text: Does a prescription need to be part of the submission? What happens if it isn't, and does a prescription arriving later change the patient's enrollment in any way?
Besides sending an off-label form back to the office, in what ways can a submission end without the patient being enrolled? Is anyone notified when that happens?
When something is missing from the form, is it always the office that gets chased, or does the patient sometimes get contacted too? How is that decided?

transcript.text: yes it needs to be part of submission. IT never isn't. No cases like this exist. The office will get chased, as well as the patient. A maximum of three times before the enrollment is cancelled.

Thanks — I'll keep moving through the main line toward the hand-off to benefits investigation, since the flow is thinnest at that end. Let me ask about whether anyone reaches out to the patient once they're enrolled, and how benefits investigation gets started.

questions.text: Once a patient is enrolled, is there a welcome contact with them? If so, who makes it and when — and what happens if the patient can't be reached?
When a patient moves on to BV, can benefits investigation start while parts of enrollment are still outstanding, or does everything have to be in place first?
Can a patient be partly enrolled — receiving some support before everything is in place — or is it all or nothing?

transcript.text:
Thanks for working through all of that. We've covered a lot, and here's what's still open if you'd like to fill any of it in:

Main flow
- Where new work lands before Meridian picks it up
- What record is first created when the PEF is keyed
- How the prescriber is found and linked
- Whether a patient can be partly enrolled
- Whether there's a welcome contact once enrolled
- Whether benefits investigation can start before enrollment is fully complete
- The ways a submission can end without the patient enrolled

Duplicate handling
- How Meridian confirms a match and what the outcomes are

Off-label review
- Whether the prescriber is ever contacted about the diagnosis

Missing information (HCP)
- Whether the three attempts are for the office alone or shared across both parties
- What happens when the office doesn't respond — any escalation

Missing information (patient)
- Who contacts the patient
- Whether the three attempts are for the patient alone or shared
- What happens when the patient doesn't respond

Would you like to pick any of these up, or shall we finish here?
